passage:
I'm Alka, the classroom assistant. On Tuesday Bhupen kept saying, "Teacher, do it for me," when it was time to write his name. I can't be sure why, but he kept glancing at the teacher's face and his pencil hand stayed still.
The teacher crouched beside him. "Try one step, and I will be here."
Bhupen wrote a wobbly B, then looked up. The teacher nodded and stayed close, saying nothing. He wrote the rest slowly and held up the page.
The teacher smiled, and Bhupen let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Bhupen keep saying when it was time to write his name?
qa.a: He kept saying, "Teacher, do it for me."

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when he asked for help with his name?
qa.a: He may have been afraid of failing and wanted to feel safe, though Alka says she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Bhupen learn?
qa.a: They asked for one step, stayed close, and let him finish on his own, which is neither too much help nor too little.

qa.q: How might Alka see the teacher's way of helping?
qa.a: Alka seems to notice that staying near but not taking over let Bhupen finish, reporting it calmly step by step.

grounding: A child keeps asking the teacher to do it for him out of fear of failing, and the teacher says try one step and I will be here.

passage:
Note from Kalyani Ma'am, class teacher, to Hemant's parents.
All week Hemant has asked me to do his cutting for him. "Ma'am, you do it. Mine will go wrong." He holds the scissors out and looks scared. Today I did not take them. I said, "Try one step. Just cut to the first line. I'll be right here." His hand shook a little. He cut to the line. I said, "One step done." He tried the next one himself. His star was wobbly, but he held it up and grinned. I will keep helping a little less each day.

qa.q: What did Hemant ask Kalyani Ma'am to do?
qa.a: He asked her to do his cutting for him.

qa.q: Why did Hemant keep asking the teacher to do it?
qa.a: He felt scared of getting it wrong and wanted to feel safe by letting her do it.

qa.q: What did Kalyani Ma'am do that balances too much and too little help?
qa.a: She didn't take the scissors but broke the task into one small step and stayed right beside him.

qa.q: How might Hemant's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel glad and hopeful, seeing Hemant grow braver with the teacher's steady support.

grounding: A young boy keeps asking his teacher to do things for him out of fear of failing, and she coaxes him to try one step while she stays close.

passage: In the one-room village school, the children were writing the letter "ka" on their slates. Mridul held his chalk out to Abhinav Sir. "Sir, you write it. Mine will be bad." His eyes were wet. Abhinav Sir sat down on the floor beside him. "Try only the first curve. I'll be right here." Mridul pressed the chalk and made a small curve. "Good. Now the line." Mridul made the line. It was crooked. He looked up, worried. "That's a ka," said Sir. "Your ka." Mridul looked at it, then rubbed it out and tried again, by himself.

qa.q: What letter were the children writing?
How was Mridul feeling when he held out his chalk?
qa.a: He felt afraid of failing, his eyes wet, and wanted Sir to do it so it would be safe.

qa.q: What did Abhinav Sir say that helped Mridul try?
qa.a: He said to try only the first curve and that he would be right there, then praised the crooked letter as Mridul's own.

qa.q: What would change if Abhinav Sir wrote it for Mridul every time?
qa.a: Mridul would stay scared and not learn to write it himself.

grounding: A young boy asks his teacher to write for him because he fears failing, and the teacher helps him try one step at a time.
